source.title: Data and Parameter Scaling Laws for Neural Machine Translation
source.authors: Mitchell A. Gordon; Kevin Duh; Jared Kaplan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law scaling and extrapolation in supervised neural machine translation, a different training regime from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling results for supervised NMT. It does not sweep training compute or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It does not report a controlled fixed-parameter comparison of architecture shapes. Raw point values shown only in plots are not transcribed here. The BLEU–development-loss relationship is recorded as a related finding, not as a test of downstream performance from language-model pretraining.
record.test_reason: The study, which is not an original source, fits its own Kaplan-style L(N,D) power laws to supervised Transformer NMT development loss. It also tests whether exponents fitted on 3–6% of the data match full-data fits and reports where the power law breaks down. This bears on V5 (a new training regime), on V2 and V7 within that regime, and weakly on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors additionally claim that fits on small data subsets precisely predict systems trained on orders of magnitude more data. They also say they do not investigate which training factors set the exponents.
record.recipe_differences: Supervised neural machine translation rather than language-model pretraining; development cross-entropy rather than held-out pretraining loss; parameter and data sweeps, with no compute-optimal allocation experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The low-data trend changes with BPE vocabulary size (30k versus 2k). In the Japanese-English retrospective analysis, BPE vocabulary and layer count affect the fitted constant multiplier, while attention-head settings 8 and 16 do not seem to affect the trend. The authors also exclude some large-loss outliers associated with specific learning rates and suspected non-convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Within a fixed language pair and BPE setting, BLEU rises exponentially as development cross-entropy falls. The relationship is noisy below BLEU 15, and BPE changes the constant C but not k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In supervised NMT, BLEU ≈ C·exp(−kL) of development loss, with k stable across BPE encodings.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The main experiments cover three language pairs and supervised NMT, not language-model pretraining. The paper says the low-resource BLEU/cross-entropy relationship is noisy and that its predictions have limited precision and reliability. Some Japanese-English large-loss outliers are excluded as suspected non-convergence. No causal explanation is tested.
record.rows_left_out: No reportable claim-relevant result was omitted. Individual plot-point values were not extracted where the text provides only figures; qualitative findings stated in the text and captions are recorded.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models. Only supervised NMT development loss is measured. Compute is not swept.
Extrapolation in parameters or compute. Extrapolation over several orders of magnitude. Direct loss prediction for held-out large runs; only exponent stability is reported.
A quantitative fixed-parameter depth/width comparison. The size of the layer-count effect on N_C.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Compute scaling. Data scaling for Japanese-English.
Everything: downstream tasks as a function of LM scale or pretraining loss.
Parameter counting, training schedule, fitting method, and disagreement between compute-optimal splits.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan is a co-author, but this paper is not one of the listed originals. The parameter range is about 2 orders of magnitude (393k–56M) and the data range about 3 (40k–50M lines). Pure-power-law exponents and fit quality come only from Figure 1; no residuals are reported. Linking R4–R9 to V2 treats V2 as applying in the NMT regime; a stricter reading would confine these rows to V5.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures supervised NMT development loss, not held-out pretraining loss of language models.
Tests extrapolation across NMT data sizes, not language-model runs orders of magnitude larger in parameters or compute.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
The study does not compare loss at a fixed parameter count across architecture shapes.
Tests supervised text-to-text NMT only; no image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer setting.
Does not test downstream-task performance as a function of language-model scale or language-model pretraining loss.
Does not test compute-optimal splits or disagreement between published compute-optimal laws; it examines NMT scaling fits, selected setup changes, and a low-data curve breakdown.

rows.baseline: Power-law trend at larger data sizes
rows.value: The scaling curve breaks down and plateaus at an apparent ceiling of 7.8 nats.
rows.note: The authors caution against extrapolating losses near or above unigram-language-model performance.
rows.check: V2 was added because the authors say the breakdown casts doubt on extrapolation. 'Absent' refers to the power law (V2/V5). For V7 the bend away from a single power law is observed. Figure 3's language pair is unstated; it is likely de-en, since the appendix covers ru-en and zh-en.

source_check.correct: V5: absent power-law behavior in this regime; V7: observed vocabulary-dependent bend. For V2, the text explicitly questions extrapolation but does not report an extrapolation-error measurement.
source_check.problem: A single absent state does not fit all linked versions: the breakdown is positive evidence for V7.

conditions.value: BPE vocabulary size and number of layers varied

rows.measure: Power-law fit and scaling coefficient behavior
rows.baseline: Other configurations in the retrospective analysis
rows.value: Power-law scaling is reported; BPE vocabulary size and layer count can change the constant multiplier, but do not seem to change αN much.
rows.note: The text excludes some large-loss outliers associated with specific learning rates and suspected non-convergence.
rows.check: V4 was added. Layer count shifts N_C at a given N, so shape changes loss, but the size of the shift is not stated: cannot_determine for V4. For V7, only the constant changes, not α_N (partial). The data uses a single dataset size (footnote 12). Outliers were excluded.

source_check.correct: V5: observed parameter power law; V7: partial, because N_C changes while alpha_N appears stable; V4: cannot_determine, because the loss effect of changing layer count at fixed parameter count is not quantified.
source_check.problem: Observed fits V5 but overstates the evidence for V7 and V4.

rows.value: The head settings do not seem to affect scaling trends.
rows.note: The study reports no material difference between the 8- and 16-head settings.
rows.check: V4 was added: head count is an architecture detail at a fixed parameter count, and 'absent' (no effect) means the row is observed for V4. For V7, no dependence on this choice was found. The evidence is qualitative only.

source_check.correct: V4: observed architectural insensitivity for 8 versus 16 heads; V5: observed parameter-scaling trends in this analysis; V7: absent dependence on head count.
